Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette: Mark, a 45-year-old European American journalist, has been struggling with symptoms that began shortly after his captivity experience. During those harrowing weeks in captivity, he was subjected to intense physical and psychological torture, which left deep emotional and physical scars. Since his release, Mark's memories of the traumatic event have become overwhelming. His mind is plagued by vivid replays of the frightening moments, like a film that plays over and over again. These memories force their way into his consciousness without warning, especially when he encounters certain triggers. For example, any neck pain immediately transports him back to the painful sensations he felt during those torturous sessions. When he smells alcohol, which was used as part of the torture process, Mark's mind is flooded with distressing images that bring back the same terror he experienced at the time. Mark has developed a high level of hypervigilance and reacts strongly to any unexpected or loud sounds, often interpreting them as immediate threats. This heightened state of alertness has led to frequent false alarms where he believes he is in danger even when there is no real threat. His hypervigilant state exacerbates his memories; every time he hears a sudden noise, it triggers the same overwhelming sense of fear and trauma that he experienced during captivity. Consequently, these heightened states often lead to a resurgence of painful memories. His occupation as a journalist adds another layer of difficulty. Working in an environment where he is frequently exposed to various sounds and physical interactions has made his condition more challenging. Mark's colleagues have noticed that he reacts strongly when they accidentally touch him or work too closely together, leading to strained professional relationships. His wife also observes the tension at home, particularly during social gatherings where the smell of alcohol can set off a series of flashbacks. Mark's hypervigilance has become a self-reinforcing cycle. The more he is on high alert, the more likely he is to experience false alarms, which in turn intensify his intrusive memories and trigger reactions like neck pain or panic at the sound of unexpected noises. This constant state of fear and reliving trauma has significantly impacted his ability to function both professionally and personally. The relentless cycle of hypervigilance leading to memory intrusions and subsequent triggering sensations has become overwhelming for Mark. He finally sought help when he realized that these symptoms were not only affecting him but also causing strain in his relationships with colleagues and family members. What frightens him most is the fear of never fully recovering from this traumatic experience, while what he hopes for is a way to regain control over his life and find peace without the constant specter of trauma looming over every moment.
